newsitem.title: UK: Chemical tape measure to transform hunt for oil.
newsitem.headline: Chemical tape measure to transform hunt for oil.

text.p: A remarkable set of "chemical milometers" have been discovered that will revolutionise the search for crude oil.
"It is a breakthrough in petroleum geochemistry," said Math Kohnen, a geochemist at Shell's Research department in the Netherlands.

"We are still in the early days but there are already clear applications," he said, adding that his company had already employed the technique, which gives clues to where oil reserves are hidden, in the North Sea and the Middle East.
"We already use this method in-house. If I see a useful application in the search for petroleum, anywhere in the world, I will advise them to use it."

Research led by Professor Stephen Larter of Newcastle University in England, the results of which were published last October in the British scientific journal Nature, has uncovered two chemicals which exist in trace elements in oil and which migrate away from oil deposits through the surrounding geology at different speeds.

By measuring the relative concentrations of these compounds, known as benzocarbazoles, it is possible to measure how far the oil has migrated from its source -- even at distances of hundreds of kilometres (miles.)

"People have been looking for compounds that would do this for a very long time," Larter said. He added that while other chemical markers for oil had been known about for 20 years, "the missing link has been measuring the distance."
"We have now added a molecular marker for migration."
The method is far cheaper than other methods of petroleum exploration such as seismics.

"This technique will never replace seismic data," Kohnen said, "but it could enhance the likelihood of finding petroleum in a particular structure. Seismic data do not often directly indicate the actual presence of petroleum."

The Catch-22 problem, according to Idar Horstad, a senior geologist at Norway's Norsk Hydro ASA, is that because not enough research data has yet been collected from around the world, it is not yet possible fully to refine, or calibrate the technique.
And because the science is still immature, many companies are still reluctant to use it, and thus to produce data.
"As more groups around the world start to apply the technique, you will get more and more data from around the world and that means you can start to calibrate the system," Horstad said.

The technique is already being used successfully in areas such as the North Sea, where oil production from a number of mature fields is already in decline but also a lot of information about the geological structures is already available.
Companies are obviously keen to squeeze more oil out of these mature areas.
"It can enable the improved ranking of prospects according to the probability of success in finding petroleum," Kohnen said.
"One application of this technology is aimed at the location of smaller petroleum reserves near existing large fields, such as in the North Sea."
But for certain areas, the science does not yet work as well.
"Where the interpretation (of the data) is not clear, it does not necessarily mean that the technique does not work, it could merely mean that we do not understand the petroleum system fully.
